blocks.prompt: 3 (i) Use the factor theorem to determine if the first polynomial is a factor of the second polynomial: \(x + 1\), \(x^{2} - 1\).
blocks.explanation:
A yes/no question: is \(x + 1\) a factor of \(x^{2} - 1\)?
Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor exactly when \(f(a) = 0\).
Plan: find \(a\), work out \(f(a)\), decide, and confirm by synthetic division.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2} - 1\), possible factor \(x + 1\).
To find: whether \(x + 1\) is a factor.
Method: Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor of \(f(x)\) if and only if \(f(a) = 0\).

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x + 1 = x - (-1)\]
\[a = -1\]
Why: The theorem needs the form \(x - a\); a plus sign in the divisor means \(a\) is negative.

Work out \(f(-1)\)
\[f(-1) = (-1)^{2} - 1\]
\[= 1 - 1\]
\[= 0\]
Why: An even power of a negative number is positive and an odd power is negative.

Decide
\[f(-1) = 0\]
So \(x + 1\) is a factor of \(x^{2} - 1\).
Why: Remainder 0 means the division is exact; this is the factor theorem.

Check: synthetic division by \(x + 1\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrr} -1 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\  &  & -1 & 1 \\ \hline & 1 & -1 & \boxed{0} \end{array}\]
\[x^{2} - 1 = (x + 1)(x - 1)\]
Why: The remainder (boxed) is 0 and the other bottom numbers give the quotient \(x - 1\).

blocks.prompt: 3 (ii) Use the factor theorem to determine if the first polynomial is a factor of the second polynomial: \(x - 2\), \(x^{2} - 5x + 6\).
blocks.explanation:
A yes/no question: is \(x - 2\) a factor of \(x^{2} - 5x + 6\)?
Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor exactly when \(f(a) = 0\).
Plan: find \(a\), work out \(f(a)\), decide, and confirm by synthetic division.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2} - 5x + 6\), possible factor \(x - 2\).
To find: whether \(x - 2\) is a factor.
Method: Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor of \(f(x)\) if and only if \(f(a) = 0\).

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x - 2 = x - a\]
\[a = 2\]
Why: The remainder theorem is stated for a divisor of the form \(x - a\).

Work out \(f(2)\)
\[f(2) = (2)^{2} - 5(2) + 6\]
\[= 4 - 10 + 6\]
\[= 0\]
Why: Work out each power first, then multiply by the coefficient.

Decide
\[f(2) = 0\]
So \(x - 2\) is a factor of \(x^{2} - 5x + 6\).
Why: Remainder 0 means the division is exact; this is the factor theorem.

Check: synthetic division by \(x - 2\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrr} 2 & 1 & -5 & 6 \\  &  & 2 & -6 \\ \hline & 1 & -3 & \boxed{0} \end{array}\]
\[x^{2} - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)\]
Why: The remainder (boxed) is 0 and the other bottom numbers give the quotient \(x - 3\).

blocks.prompt: 3 (iii) Use the factor theorem to determine if the first polynomial is a factor of the second polynomial: \(x + 1\), \(x^{3} + x^{2} + x - 3\).
blocks.explanation:
A yes/no question: is \(x + 1\) a factor of \(x^{3} + x^{2} + x - 3\)?
Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor exactly when \(f(a) = 0\).
Plan: find \(a\), work out \(f(a)\), decide, and confirm by synthetic division.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{3} + x^{2} + x - 3\), possible factor \(x + 1\).
To find: whether \(x + 1\) is a factor.
Method: Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor of \(f(x)\) if and only if \(f(a) = 0\).

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x + 1 = x - (-1)\]
\[a = -1\]
Why: The theorem needs the form \(x - a\); a plus sign in the divisor means \(a\) is negative.

Work out \(f(-1)\)
\[f(-1) = (-1)^{3} + (-1)^{2} + (-1) - 3\]
\[= -1 + 1 - 1 - 3\]
\[= -4\]
Why: An even power of a negative number is positive and an odd power is negative.

Decide
\[f(-1) = -4 \ne 0\]
So \(x + 1\) is not a factor of \(x^{3} + x^{2} + x - 3\).
Why: By the factor theorem, \(x + 1\) is a factor only if \(f(-1)\) is 0. Here a remainder \(-4\) is left.

Check: synthetic division by \(x + 1\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrr} -1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & -3 \\  &  & -1 & 0 & -1 \\ \hline & 1 & 0 & 1 & \boxed{-4} \end{array}\]
Why: The boxed remainder is \(-4\), not 0, which agrees with \(f(-1)\).
blocks.final_answer: No, \(x + 1\) is not a factor of \(x^{3} + x^{2} + x - 3\) (remainder \(-4\)).

blocks.prompt: 3 (iv) Use the factor theorem to determine if the first polynomial is a factor of the second polynomial: \(x - 2\), \(x^{3} + x^{2} - 7x + 2\).
blocks.explanation:
A yes/no question: is \(x - 2\) a factor of \(x^{3} + x^{2} - 7x + 2\)?
Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor exactly when \(f(a) = 0\).
Plan: find \(a\), work out \(f(a)\), decide, and confirm by synthetic division.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{3} + x^{2} - 7x + 2\), possible factor \(x - 2\).
To find: whether \(x - 2\) is a factor.
Method: Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor of \(f(x)\) if and only if \(f(a) = 0\).

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x - 2 = x - a\]
\[a = 2\]
Why: The remainder theorem is stated for a divisor of the form \(x - a\).

Work out \(f(2)\)
\[f(2) = (2)^{3} + (2)^{2} - 7(2) + 2\]
\[= 8 + 4 - 14 + 2\]
\[= 0\]
Why: Work out each power first, then multiply by the coefficient.

Decide
\[f(2) = 0\]
So \(x - 2\) is a factor of \(x^{3} + x^{2} - 7x + 2\).
Why: Remainder 0 means the division is exact; this is the factor theorem.

Check: synthetic division by \(x - 2\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrr} 2 & 1 & 1 & -7 & 2 \\  &  & 2 & 6 & -2 \\ \hline & 1 & 3 & -1 & \boxed{0} \end{array}\]
\[x^{3} + x^{2} - 7x + 2 = (x - 2)(x^{2} + 3x - 1)\]
Why: The remainder (boxed) is 0 and the other bottom numbers give the quotient \(x^{2} + 3x - 1\).
blocks.final_answer: Yes, \(x - 2\) is a factor of \(x^{3} + x^{2} - 7x + 2\).

blocks.prompt: 3 (v) Use the factor theorem to determine if the first polynomial is a factor of the second polynomial: \(x - 3\), \(x^{4} - 3x^{3} + x^{2} - x + 1\).
blocks.explanation:
A yes/no question: is \(x - 3\) a factor of \(x^{4} - 3x^{3} + x^{2} - x + 1\)?
Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor exactly when \(f(a) = 0\).
Plan: find \(a\), work out \(f(a)\), decide, and confirm by synthetic division.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{4} - 3x^{3} + x^{2} - x + 1\), possible factor \(x - 3\).
To find: whether \(x - 3\) is a factor.
Method: Factor theorem: \(x - a\) is a factor of \(f(x)\) if and only if \(f(a) = 0\).

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x - 3 = x - a\]
\[a = 3\]
Why: The remainder theorem is stated for a divisor of the form \(x - a\).

Work out \(f(3)\)
\[f(3) = (3)^{4} - 3(3)^{3} + (3)^{2} - (3) + 1\]
\[= 81 - 81 + 9 - 3 + 1\]
\[= 7\]
Why: Work out each power first, then multiply by the coefficient.

Decide
\[f(3) = 7 \ne 0\]
So \(x - 3\) is not a factor of \(x^{4} - 3x^{3} + x^{2} - x + 1\).
Why: By the factor theorem, \(x - 3\) is a factor only if \(f(3)\) is 0. Here a remainder \(7\) is left.

Check: synthetic division by \(x - 3\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrrr} 3 & 1 & -3 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\  &  & 3 & 0 & 3 & 6 \\ \hline & 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & \boxed{7} \end{array}\]
Why: The boxed remainder is \(7\), not 0, which agrees with \(f(3)\).
blocks.final_answer: No, \(x - 3\) is not a factor of \(x^{4} - 3x^{3} + x^{2} - x + 1\) (remainder \(7\)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key labels the last two answers of Question 3 both "(iv)". The second "(iv)" (\(x - 3\) is not a factor of \(x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 - x + 1\)) is part (v). The answers themselves are correct.
